claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claims.claim: The mTwf1 tail peptide displayed high affinity, concentration-dependent binding to CPα1β2.
claims.source: The mTwf1 tail peptide displayed high affinity, concentration-dependent binding to CPα1β2, a major non-muscle isoform of CP in mammalian cells (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Full-length mTwf1 protein competed with the labeled mTwf1 tail for CP binding.
claims.source: Moreover, full-length mTwf1 protein (unlabeled) competed with the labeled mTwf1 tail for CP binding, whereas full-length mTwf1-11 (unlabeled) did not (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy competition data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Full-length mTwf1-11 did not compete with the labeled mTwf1 tail for CP binding.
claims.source: Moreover, full-length mTwf1 protein (unlabeled) competed with the labeled mTwf1 tail for CP binding, whereas full-length mTwf1-11 (unlabeled) did not (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy competition data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The mTwf1-11 mutant effectively uncouples mTwf1 binding to CP.
claims.source: Thus, the mTwf1-11 mutant effectively uncouples mTwf1 binding to CP.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data showing mTwf1-11 does not compete for CP binding (Figure 1C).

claims.claim: 1 µM mTwf1 accelerated barbed end depolymerization by 2–3 fold compared to control reactions.
claims.source: In agreement with previous observations using yeast and mouse Twinfilin (Hilton et al., 2018; Johnston et al., 2015), 1 µM mTwf1 accelerated barbed end depolymerization by 2–3 fold compared to control reactions (Figure 1D), and the addition of CP blocked this effect (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The addition of CP blocked the mTwf1-mediated acceleration of barbed end depolymerization.
claims.source: In agreement with previous observations using yeast and mouse Twinfilin (Hilton et al., 2018; Johnston et al., 2015), 1 µM mTwf1 accelerated barbed end depolymerization by 2–3 fold compared to control reactions (Figure 1D), and the addition of CP blocked this effect (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: mTwf1-11 exhibited a similar depolymerization rate to wild-type mTwf1.
claims.source: Further, mTwf1-11 exhibited a similar rate (Figure 1D), indicating that this mutant has wild type depolymerization activity, and thus separates Twinfilin's ability to bind CP from its ability to promote barbed-end depolymerization.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The mTwf1-11 mutant has wild type depolymerization activity.
claims.source: Further, mTwf1-11 exhibited a similar rate (Figure 1D), indicating that this mutant has wild type depolymerization activity, and thus separates Twinfilin's ability to bind CP from its ability to promote barbed-end depolymerization.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the similar depolymerization rates observed for mTwf1 and mTwf1-11 (Figure 1D).

claims.claim: The addition of CP was able to block barbed-end depolymerization by mTwf1-11.
claims.source: Interestingly, the addition of CP was still able to block barbed-end depolymerization by mTwf1-11 (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: CP sterically blocks mTwf1 access to barbed ends, independent of its direct interaction with mTwf1.
claims.source: These observations suggest that CP sterically blocks mTwf1 access to barbed ends, independent of its direct interaction with mTwf1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CP blocks both mTwf1 and mTwf1-11 depolymerization activity (Figure 1E).

claims.claim: The mTwf1 tail interacted equally well with wild-type CP and CPαΔ28.
claims.source: Importantly, in binding assays the mTwf1 tail interacted equally well with wild-type CP and CPαΔ28, demonstrating that this mutant binds normally to mTwf1 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Equimolar amounts of CPαΔ28 did not significantly alter mTwf1 depolymerization activity.
claims.source: In TIRF assays, equimolar amounts of CPαΔ28 did not significantly alter mTwf1 depolymerization activity (Figure 1F; Figure 1—video 1; also summarized in Figure 1G), suggesting that while CP blocks Twinfilin access to barbed ends, Twinfilin-CP direct interaction does not alter Twinfilin depolymerization activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1F and summarized in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: While CP blocks Twinfilin access to barbed ends, Twinfilin-CP direct interaction does not alter Twinfilin depolymerization activity.
claims.source: In TIRF assays, equimolar amounts of CPαΔ28 did not significantly alter mTwf1 depolymerization activity (Figure 1F; Figure 1—video 1; also summarized in Figure 1G), suggesting that while CP blocks Twinfilin access to barbed ends, Twinfilin-CP direct interaction does not alter Twinfilin depolymerization activity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CPαΔ28 (which binds mTwf1 but doesn't cap) doesn't affect mTwf1 depolymerization activity (Figure 1F-G).

claims.claim: The C-terminal tail regions of evolutionarily diverse Twinfilins share sequence homology with the CPI motifs of several CPI family proteins.
claims.source: We were particularly interested in how Twinfilin might impact the regulation of CP by CPI-motif proteins such as CARMIL, since we noticed that the C-terminal tail regions of evolutionarily diverse Twinfilins share sequence homology with the CPI motifs of several CPI family proteins (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The consensus CPI motif is 17-amino acids long.
claims.source: The consensus CPI motif is 17-amino acids long, with some additional contacts contributed from outside this motif, and tolerates significant divergence across the CPI-motif family (Edwards et al., 2014; Hernandez-Valladares et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Edwards et al., 2014 and Hernandez-Valladares et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The CP(RY) mutant is insensitive to inhibition and uncapping by CARMIL.
claims.source: The CP(RY) mutant is insensitive to inhibition and uncapping by CARMIL and disrupts binding with at least two other CPI-motif proteins, CD2AP and WASHCAP (FAM21) (Edwards et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Edwards et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The CP(RY) mutant disrupts binding with CD2AP and WASHCAP (FAM21).
claims.source: The CP(RY) mutant is insensitive to inhibition and uncapping by CARMIL and disrupts binding with at least two other CPI-motif proteins, CD2AP and WASHCAP (FAM21) (Edwards et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Edwards et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The CP(RY) mutant has approximately 20-fold reduced affinity for mTwf1 tail compared to wild type CP.
claims.source: In fluorescence anisotropy binding assays, we observed that the CP(RY) mutant has approximately 20-fold reduced affinity for mTwf1 tail compared to wild type CP (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: mTwf1 and CPI-motif proteins share at least partially overlapping binding sites on CP.
claims.source: These data are consistent with mTwf1 and CPI-motif proteins sharing at least partially overlapping binding sites on CP.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced binding of mTwf1 tail to CP(RY) mutant (Figure 2B).

claims.claim: The mutant (K325A) mTwf1 tail peptide showed an ~30 fold reduction in binding affinity for CP compared to wild type peptide.
claims.source: In fluorescence anisotropy binding assays, we compared the abilities of wild-type and mutant (K325A) mTwf1 tail peptides to compete with labeled mTwf1 tail peptide for CP binding. This analysis revealed an ~30 fold reduction in binding affinity for the mutant (K325A) mTwf1 tail peptide compared to wild type peptide (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy competition data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Unlabeled CBR peptide competed with the fluorescent mTwf1 tail probe for CP binding.
claims.source: We next asked whether the CP-binding region (CBR) of CARMIL1 (residues 964 – 1078) competes with mTwf1 tail for binding to CP. We observed that unlabeled CBR peptide competed with the fluorescent mTwf1 tail probe for CP binding (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy competition data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: CARMIL and mTwf1 directly compete for binding CP.
claims.source: These results indicate that CARMIL and mTwf1 directly compete for binding CP.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the competition data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Only the CPI-motif peptide and not the CSI peptide competed with mTwf1 tail for CP binding.
claims.source: As expected based on Twinfilin's sequence similarity to CPI motifs, only the CPI-motif peptide and not the CSI peptide competed with mTwf1 tail for CP binding (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy competition data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Twinfilin is a divergent CPI-motif protein.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that Twinfilin is a divergent CPI-motif protein and has important implications for CP regulation in cells (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the collective binding and competition data (Figures 2A-D).

claims.claim: Increasing concentrations of mTwf1 attenuated CARMIL's uncapping effects.
claims.source: CARMIL1 alone (no mTwf1) strongly induced uncapping, leading to the rapid polymerization of previously-capped filament seeds (Figure 3A). However, increasing concentrations of mTwf1 attenuated CARMIL's uncapping effects (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pyrene actin assembly assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: mTwf1 competes with CARMIL for binding CP, thereby blocking uncapping.
claims.source: These results are consistent with mTwf1 competing with CARMIL for binding CP, and thereby blocking uncapping.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the pyrene actin assembly data (Figure 3A).

claims.claim: CARMIL1 CBR led to the rapid displacement of SNAP-649-CP, with complete loss of CP from barbed ends by 100 s.
claims.source: As expected, in the absence of other factors, SNAP-649-CP had a long dwell time, remaining on barbed ends for tens of minutes (Figure 3B and C). However, when CARMIL1 CBR was introduced, this led to the rapid displacement of SNAP-649-CP, with complete loss of CP from barbed ends by 100 s (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and quantified in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The addition of mTwf1 with CARMIL1 CBR attenuated the uncapping effects in a concentration-dependent manner.
claims.source: The addition of mTwf1 with CARMIL1 CBR attenuated the uncapping effects in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and quantified in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The attenuation of CARMIL uncapping by Twinfilin required direct interactions between Twinfilin and CP.
claims.source: Further, this attenuation required direct interactions between Twinfilin and CP, as mTwf1-11 failed to protect CP from CARMIL uncapping (Figure 3D and E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data showing mTwf1-11 does not protect CP from CARMIL uncapping (Figure 3D-E).

claims.claim: mTwf1-11 failed to protect CP from CARMIL uncapping.
claims.source: Further, this attenuation required direct interactions between Twinfilin and CP, as mTwf1-11 failed to protect CP from CARMIL uncapping (Figure 3D and E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: Similar protective effects against CARMIL uncapping were observed for mTwf2a.
claims.source: Similar effects were observed for the other major isoform of mouse Twinfilin that is expressed in non-muscle cells, mTwf2a (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Nevalainen et al., 2011; Vartiainen et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: V-1 does not displace CP from barbed ends; instead, it sequesters CP and blocks it from binding filament ends.
claims.source: Unlike CARMIL, V-1 does not displace CP from barbed ends; instead, it sequesters CP and blocks it from binding filament ends (Bhattacharya et al., 2006; Jung et al., 2016; Taoka et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bhattacharya et al., 2006; Jung et al., 2016; Taoka et al., 2003.

claims.claim: V-1 interacts with CP on the opposite face from CARMIL, sterically blocking binding to the filament end.
claims.source: In contrast to the CARMIL binding site on CP, which partially encircles the 'stalk' of the CP heterodimer (Hernandez-Valladares et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2018; Zwolak et al., 2010), V-1 interacts with CP on the opposite face, sterically blocking binding to the filament end (Johnson et al., 2018; Takeda et al., 2010; Zwolak et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2018; Takeda et al., 2010; Zwolak et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The addition of V-1 to CP-capped filament seeds restored actin assembly to uncapped levels.
claims.source: As expected, filament seeds pre-incubated with CP and then mixed with pyrene-actin monomers displayed minimal growth, whereas the addition of V-1 restored actin assembly to uncapped levels.
claims.evidence: This is based on pyrene-actin seeded elongation assays (Figure 4A).

claims.claim: The further addition of mTwf1 suppressed V-1's effects, restoring capping activity.
claims.source: Somewhat to our surprise, the further addition of mTwf1 suppressed V-1's effects, restoring capping activity, while mTwf1-11 had no effect (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pyrene-actin seeded elongation assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: mTwf1-11 had no effect on V-1's inhibition of CP.
claims.source: Somewhat to our surprise, the further addition of mTwf1 suppressed V-1's effects, restoring capping activity, while mTwf1-11 had no effect (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pyrene-actin seeded elongation assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Even high concentrations of V-1 (1000-fold excess to mTwf1 tail probe) fail to compete with mTwf1 for CP binding.
claims.source: These effects were unexpected given the above-mentioned differences in Twinfilin's predicted and V-1's known binding sites on CP, and our observation that even high concentrations of V-1 (1000-fold excess to mTwf1 tail probe) fail to compete with mTwf1 for CP binding in anisotropy assays (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: mTwf1 attenuates V-1 effects on CP via an allosteric mechanism, distinct from a simple steric binding competition.
claims.source: These results suggest that mTwf1 attenuates V-1 effects on CP via an allosteric mechanism, distinct from a simple steric binding competition.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that V-1 doesn't compete with mTwf1 for CP binding (Figure 4C) yet mTwf1 affects V-1 function (Figure 4A).

claims.claim: CARMIL forms a transient ternary complex with V-1 and CP, leading to accelerated dissociation of V-1 from CP.
claims.source: In probing the mechanism further, we drew inspiration from a study by Fujiwara and colleagues, showing that CARMIL forms a transient ternary complex with V-1 and CP, leading to accelerated dissociation of V-1 from CP (Fujiwara et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fujiwara et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The rate of V-1 dissociation from CP increased in the presence of increasing concentrations of mTwf1.
claims.source: The rate of V-1 dissociation from CP increased in the presence of increasing concentrations of mTwf1, pointing to the possible formation of a transient ternary complex that destabilizes V-1 interactions with CP (Figure 4D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by stopped-flow fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claims.claim: mTwf1-11 failed to enhance V-1 dissociation from CP.
claims.source: Importantly, mTwf1-11 failed to enhance V-1 dissociation (Figure 4E), showing that this effect depends on direct interactions between mTwf1 tail and CP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by stopped-flow fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The effect of mTwf1 on V-1 dissociation depends on direct interactions between mTwf1 tail and CP.
claims.source: Importantly, mTwf1-11 failed to enhance V-1 dissociation (Figure 4E), showing that this effect depends on direct interactions between mTwf1 tail and CP.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mTwf1-11 (which doesn't bind CP) doesn't enhance V-1 dissociation (Figure 4E).

claims.claim: CARMIL and Twinfilin share a common function in catalyzing the dissociation of V-1 from CP using their CPI motifs to bind CP.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that CARMIL and Twinfilin share a common function in catalyzing the dissociation of V-1 from CP using their CPI motifs to bind CP, despite having different effects on the displacement of CP from barbed ends.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the collective data showing both CARMIL and Twinfilin accelerate V-1 dissociation from CP.

claims.claim: The presence of mTwf1 resulted in protection from H-D exchange at the N-terminal stalk of CP.
claims.source: The results were essentially the same in each case. The presence of mTwf1 resulted in protection from H-D exchange at the N-terminal stalk of CP (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Similar H-D exchange protection effects were observed upon CARMIL binding to CP.
claims.source: Similar effects to H-D exchange were observed upon CARMIL binding to CP (Johnson et al., 2018); also shown here in Figure 5B), which correspond well with the CPI-motif binding site defined by X-ray crystallography and solution NMR studies (Hernandez-Valladares et al., 2010; Takeda et al., 2010; Zwolak et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2018 and HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: mTwf1 binding caused H-D exchange protection of a small region on CP corresponding to the V-1 binding site.
claims.source: For mTwf1, we also observed H-D exchange protection of a small region on CP corresponding to the V-1 binding site (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2), consistent with our results described above for the effects of mTwf1 in promoting V-1 dissociation from CP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5A-B and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: mTwf1-induced changes in CP conformation at the actin-binding interface were not as extensive as those induced by CARMIL.
claims.source: However, it is worth noting that mTwf1-induced changes in CP conformation at the actin-binding interface were not as extensive as those induced by CARMIL, which is consistent with CARMIL, but not mTwf1, weakening CP binding to actin at the barbed ends.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of HDX-MS data for mTwf1 and CARMIL binding to CP (Figure 5A-B).

claims.claim: Strong colocalization of Twinfilin and CP was observed throughout B16F10 cells with co-enrichment at the actin-rich leading and trailing edges.
claims.source: We observed strong colocalization of Twinfilin and CP throughout the cell and a co-enrichment at the actin-rich leading and trailing edges (Figure 6A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claims.claim: Twinfilin and CP are present at ~1:2 molar ratio in B16F10 cells.
claims.source: Further, quantitative western blotting showed that Twinfilin and CP are present at ~1:2 molar ratio in B16F10 cells (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative western blotting data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The concentration of CP in B16F10 cells is ~1 µM.
claims.source: Previous studies reported the concentration of CP in B16F10 cells to be ~1 µM (Fujiwara et al., 2014; Pollard and Borisy, 2003), suggesting that mTwf1 is present at ~0.5 µM.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fujiwara et al., 2014 and Pollard and Borisy, 2003.

claims.claim: mTwf1 is present at ~0.5 µM in B16F10 cells.
claims.source: Previous studies reported the concentration of CP in B16F10 cells to be ~1 µM (Fujiwara et al., 2014; Pollard and Borisy, 2003), suggesting that mTwf1 is present at ~0.5 µM.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the 1:2 molar ratio of Twinfilin to CP (Figure 6C) and the reported CP concentration of ~1 µM.

claims.claim: The Twinfilin-CP interaction has a Kd of 50 nM.
claims.source: Given the high affinity of the Twinfilin-CP interaction (Kd = 50 nM), these observations are consistent with mTwf1 being associated with a substantial fraction of the CP in cells.
claims.evidence: This is based on binding data from the manuscript (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: mTwf1 is associated with a substantial fraction of the CP in cells.
claims.source: Given the high affinity of the Twinfilin-CP interaction (Kd = 50 nM), these observations are consistent with mTwf1 being associated with a substantial fraction of the CP in cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the high affinity of the interaction (Kd = 50 nM) and the cellular concentrations of both proteins.

claims.claim: Knockdown of either mTwf1 or CP led to a marked increase in the density of peripheral protrusions or microspikes with a concomitant loss of lamellipodial surfaces.
claims.source: Knockdown of either mTwf1 or CP led to a similar, marked increase in the density of peripheral protrusions or microspikes with a concomitant loss of lamellipodial surfaces (Figure 6F and G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claims.claim: Similar phenotypes have been reported for CP depletion in multiple cell lines.
claims.source: Similar phenotypes have been reported for CP depletion in multiple cell lines (Edwards et al., 2013; Edwards et al., 2015; Mejillano et al., 2004; Sinnar et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Edwards et al., 2013; Edwards et al., 2015; Mejillano et al., 2004; Sinnar et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Expression of an RNAi-refractive mTwf1 construct rescued the defects caused by depletion of endogenous mTwf1.
claims.source: Expression of an RNAi-refractive mTwf1 construct, but not mTwf1-11, rescued the defects caused by depletion of endogenous mTwf1 (Figure 6F and G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that these cellular functions of mTwf1 critically depend on its interaction with CP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claims.claim: Expression of mTwf1-11 did not rescue the defects caused by depletion of endogenous mTwf1.
claims.source: Expression of an RNAi-refractive mTwf1 construct, but not mTwf1-11, rescued the defects caused by depletion of endogenous mTwf1 (Figure 6F and G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that these cellular functions of mTwf1 critically depend on its interaction with CP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claims.claim: The cellular functions of mTwf1 critically depend on its interaction with CP.
claims.source: Expression of an RNAi-refractive mTwf1 construct, but not mTwf1-11, rescued the defects caused by depletion of endogenous mTwf1 (Figure 6F and G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that these cellular functions of mTwf1 critically depend on its interaction with CP.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that wild-type mTwf1 but not mTwf1-11 (which doesn't bind CP) rescues the knockdown phenotype.

claims.claim: Knockdown of CP was accompanied by a dramatic reduction in Twinfilin levels in cells.
claims.source: We also made the unexpected observation that knockdown of CP was accompanied by a dramatic reduction in Twinfilin levels in cells, as seen by both western blotting (Figure 6D) and immunofluorescence (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 6D and immunofluorescence data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The reduction in Twinfilin levels upon CP knockdown was confirmed using a second RNAi oligonucleotide that targets a different region of CP.
claims.source: This effect was confirmed using a second RNAi oligonucleotide that targets a different region of CP (siCP2, Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The reduction in Twinfilin levels upon CP knockdown was observed in additional cell lines besides B16F10, including Neuro-2A and NIH-3T3 cells.
claims.source: Further, it was observed in additional cell lines besides B16F10, including Neuro-2A and NIH-3T3 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Forced expression of mTwf1 partially rescued the defects associated with CP depletion.
claims.source: Forced expression of mTwf1 partially rescued the defects associated with CP depletion, indicating that a portion of the original defects observed after CP knockdown were likely due to the accompanying loss of mTwf1.
claims.evidence: This is based on rescue experiments described in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A portion of the defects observed after CP knockdown were likely due to the accompanying loss of mTwf1.
claims.source: Forced expression of mTwf1 partially rescued the defects associated with CP depletion, indicating that a portion of the original defects observed after CP knockdown were likely due to the accompanying loss of mTwf1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the partial rescue of CP knockdown phenotype by mTwf1 overexpression.

claims.claim: B16F10 cells ectopically expressing CARMIL1 showed morphological defects similar to loss of CP.
claims.source: B16F10 cells ectopically expressing CARMIL1 showed morphological defects similar to loss of CP, and ectopic mTwf1 expression rescued the defects (Figure 7A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claims.claim: Ectopic mTwf1 expression rescued the defects caused by CARMIL1 overexpression.
claims.source: B16F10 cells ectopically expressing CARMIL1 showed morphological defects similar to loss of CP, and ectopic mTwf1 expression rescued the defects (Figure 7A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of mTwf1 alone caused no significant change in cell morphology.
claims.source: Importantly, ectopic expression of mTwf1 alone caused no significant change in cell morphology.
claims.evidence: This is based on the cell morphology data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claims.claim: Twf1 promotes capping in vivo, at least in part by competing with CARMIL for CP binding and antagonizing the uncapping effects of CARMIL.
claims.source: These results support our biochemical observations, and suggest that Twf1 promotes capping in vivo, at least in part by competing with CARMIL for CP binding and antagonizing the uncapping effects of CARMIL.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue of CARMIL1 overexpression phenotype by mTwf1 (Figure 7A-B).

claims.claim: Twinfilin is a new member of the CPI-motif family of proteins.
claims.source: Taken together, these results reveal that Twinfilin is a new member of the CPI-motif family of proteins, and the first within this group to show the ability to bind CP without reducing CP affinity for barbed ends, and antagonize the negative regulatory effects of another CPI protein.
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference based on the collective data showing Twinfilin has a CPI-like motif and competes with CARMIL.

claims.claim: Twinfilin is the first CPI-motif protein to show the ability to bind CP without reducing CP affinity for barbed ends.
claims.source: Taken together, these results reveal that Twinfilin is a new member of the CPI-motif family of proteins, and the first within this group to show the ability to bind CP without reducing CP affinity for barbed ends, and antagonize the negative regulatory effects of another CPI protein.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Twinfilin binding doesn't weaken CP capping activity (Figure 1) unlike other CPI proteins.

claims.claim: Twinfilin is the first CPI-motif protein to antagonize the negative regulatory effects of another CPI protein.
claims.source: Taken together, these results reveal that Twinfilin is a new member of the CPI-motif family of proteins, and the first within this group to show the ability to bind CP without reducing CP affinity for barbed ends, and antagonize the negative regulatory effects of another CPI protein.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing Twinfilin protects CP from CARMIL (Figure 3).

claims.claim: The Fujiwara model posits that the majority of CP in the cytosol is bound to V-1, in an inactive state.
claims.source: The best working model to date has been the Fujiwara model (Fujiwara et al., 2014) (depicted here as 'Earlier Model'; Figure 7C). It posits that the majority of CP in the cytosol is bound to V-1, in an inactive state, which then can be locally 'activated' by CARMIL at the leading edge.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the Fujiwara model based on citation to Fujiwara et al., 2014.

claims.claim: In the Fujiwara model, CP can be locally 'activated' by CARMIL at the leading edge.
claims.source: The best working model to date has been the Fujiwara model (Fujiwara et al., 2014) (depicted here as 'Earlier Model'; Figure 7C). It posits that the majority of CP in the cytosol is bound to V-1, in an inactive state, which then can be locally 'activated' by CARMIL at the leading edge.

results.result: The C-terminal tail of Twinfilin contains a CPI-like motif that binds to CP at a site overlapping with CARMIL's CPI motif binding site. Sequence alignment shows homology between Twinfilin tail regions and CPI motifs across species. Mutation of conserved residues (K325A in mTwf1 tail, or R15A/Y79A in CP) reduces binding affinity by 20-30 fold. HDX-MS data demonstrates that mTwf1 binding protects the N-terminal stalk region of CP from deuterium exchange, similar to CARMIL binding.
results.evaluation: Multiple independent lines of evidence converge: sequence homology (C63, Figure 2A), mutagenesis showing specific residues are critical for binding (C67, C69), competition assays demonstrating overlapping binding sites (C72), and structural data from HDX-MS confirming similar binding regions for Twinfilin and CARMIL (C93-C95, Figure 5). The data are internally consistent and use appropriate controls including mutants that disrupt binding.

results.result: Twinfilin and CARMIL compete for binding to CP. Fluorescence anisotropy assays show that unlabeled CARMIL CBR peptide competes with fluorescent mTwf1 tail peptide for CP binding, and specifically the CPI motif (not CSI motif) of CARMIL mediates this competition.
results.evaluation: Direct competition is demonstrated by fluorescence anisotropy (C70, Figure 2D) with appropriate controls distinguishing CPI from CSI motifs (C72). The competitive binding is consistent with the overlapping binding site data from HDX-MS and mutagenesis studies. The experimental design appropriately uses labeled and unlabeled peptides to demonstrate competition.

results.result: Twinfilin protects CP from CARMIL-mediated displacement from actin filament barbed ends. In pyrene actin assembly assays and TIRF microscopy, increasing concentrations of mTwf1 attenuate CARMIL-induced uncapping in a concentration-dependent manner. This protection requires direct Twinfilin-CP interaction, as the mTwf1-11 mutant (which cannot bind CP) fails to protect CP from CARMIL uncapping.
results.evaluation: The result is supported by two independent assay types (pyrene fluorescence and TIRF microscopy, C74-C77, Figures 3A-C) showing concentration-dependent effects. Critical controls include the mTwf1-11 mutant demonstrating the requirement for direct CP binding (C78-C79, Figures 3D-E), and similar effects observed with the mTwf2a isoform (C80). The data are quantitative and reproducible across multiple experiments.

results.result: Twinfilin accelerates dissociation of the CP inhibitor V-1 from CP, restoring CP to an active capping state. This effect is concentration-dependent, requires direct Twinfilin-CP interaction (mTwf1-11 has no effect), and occurs via an allosteric mechanism rather than direct competition, as V-1 does not compete with mTwf1 for CP binding even at 1000-fold excess.
results.evaluation: Multiple complementary assays support this result: pyrene actin elongation assays show functional restoration of capping (C84-C85, Figure 4A-B), fluorescence anisotropy demonstrates lack of direct competition (C86, Figure 4C), and stopped-flow kinetics quantify accelerated V-1 dissociation (C89-C90, Figure 4D-E). The mTwf1-11 control confirms the requirement for direct CP binding (C90-C91). The allosteric mechanism is a reasonable inference given the non-overlapping binding sites.

results.result: The mTwf1 tail binds to CP with high affinity (Kd = 50 nM). Full-length mTwf1 competes with labeled mTwf1 tail for CP binding, while the mTwf1-11 mutant (K332A, R333A) does not compete, effectively uncoupling mTwf1 binding to CP. The mTwf1 tail binds equally well to wild-type CP and CPαΔ28 (a capping-deficient mutant).
results.evaluation: Fluorescence anisotropy provides quantitative binding data (C50, C101, Figure 1B) with appropriate controls including the mTwf1-11 mutant that specifically disrupts CP binding (C51-C53, Figure 1C). The CPαΔ28 control (C60) demonstrates that the tail binding is independent of CP's capping function. The Kd value is precisely determined and the mutant provides a clean separation-of-function tool used throughout the study.

results.result: CP blocks Twinfilin-mediated barbed end depolymerization by sterically occluding barbed end access, independent of direct Twinfilin-CP interaction. Both wild-type mTwf1 and the mTwf1-11 mutant (which cannot bind CP) accelerate depolymerization by 2-3 fold, but CP blocks this activity for both proteins. CPαΔ28 (which binds mTwf1 but cannot cap) does not affect mTwf1 depolymerization activity.
results.evaluation: TIRF microscopy provides direct visualization and quantification of depolymerization rates (C54-C58, Figures 1D-E). The key insight comes from the mTwf1-11 mutant: it has wild-type depolymerization activity but cannot bind CP, yet CP still blocks its activity, demonstrating steric occlusion (C58-C59). The CPαΔ28 control confirms that CP binding to mTwf1 doesn't alter depolymerization activity (C61-C62, Figure 1F-G). The logic is sound and controls are appropriate.

results.result: Knockdown of either mTwf1 or CP causes similar morphological defects in B16F10 cells, characterized by increased density of peripheral protrusions/microspikes and loss of lamellipodial surfaces. Expression of wild-type mTwf1 rescues the mTwf1 knockdown phenotype, but mTwf1-11 does not, demonstrating that cellular functions of mTwf1 critically depend on its interaction with CP.
results.evaluation: RNAi knockdown experiments show similar phenotypes for mTwf1 and CP depletion (C6, C103, Figure 6F-G), suggesting functional interdependence. The rescue experiments provide strong evidence: wild-type mTwf1 rescues but mTwf1-11 does not (C105-C106), directly demonstrating the requirement for CP binding (C107). Quantification of microspike density provides objective measurements. The use of RNAi-refractive constructs is appropriate methodology.

results.result: Elevated Twinfilin expression rescues morphological defects caused by CARMIL1 overexpression in B16F10 cells. CARMIL1 overexpression causes defects similar to CP loss, and co-expression of mTwf1 rescues these defects, while mTwf1 alone causes no significant morphological changes.
results.evaluation: Immunofluorescence and quantification show that CARMIL1 overexpression phenocopies CP loss, and mTwf1 co-expression rescues this phenotype (C113-C114, Figure 7A-B). The control showing mTwf1 alone has no effect (C115) is important for interpretation. This result provides in vivo validation of the biochemical competition between Twinfilin and CARMIL for CP binding (C116). Statistical analysis shows significant differences (p≤0.001).

results.result: Twinfilin and CP strongly colocalize throughout B16F10 cells with enrichment at actin-rich leading and trailing edges. Quantitative western blotting shows they are present at ~1:2 molar ratio, with CP at ~1 µM and mTwf1 at ~0.5 µM. Given the high affinity interaction (Kd = 50 nM), mTwf1 is likely associated with a substantial fraction of cellular CP.
results.evaluation: Immunofluorescence demonstrates colocalization with quantitative Mander's correlation coefficients (C97, Figure 6A-B). Quantitative western blotting provides stoichiometry data (C98, Figure 6C), and concentrations are based on prior literature (C99). The inference about association (C102) is reasonable given the Kd (50 nM) is 10-fold lower than the estimated cellular concentrations. The quantitative approach strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Knockdown of CP causes a dramatic reduction in Twinfilin protein levels in cells, confirmed with two independent siRNAs and observed across multiple cell lines (B16F10, Neuro-2A, NIH-3T3). Forced expression of mTwf1 partially rescues defects associated with CP depletion, suggesting some of the CP knockdown phenotype is due to accompanying Twinfilin loss.
results.evaluation: Western blotting and immunofluorescence demonstrate reduced Twinfilin upon CP knockdown (C108, Figure 6D), confirmed with a second siRNA (C109) and in multiple cell lines (C110, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The partial rescue by mTwf1 overexpression (C111-C112) supports the interpretation. This is an important observation that may require reinterpretation of prior CP knockdown studies. The use of multiple siRNAs and cell lines strengthens confidence in the result.

results.result: Twinfilin is defined as the first 'pro-capping' ligand of CP and a new member of the CPI-motif family. Unlike other CPI-motif proteins, Twinfilin binds CP without reducing its affinity for barbed ends and antagonizes the negative regulatory effects of other CPI proteins (CARMIL).
results.evaluation: This is a summary interpretation (C8, C117-C119) based on the collective experimental evidence showing: (1) Twinfilin has a CPI-like motif, (2) it protects CP from CARMIL and V-1 rather than inhibiting CP, and (3) it maintains CP's capping activity. The 'pro-capping' designation is justified by the functional data. This represents a conceptual advance in understanding CP regulation, distinguishing Twinfilin from other CPI-motif proteins.

results.result: mTwf1-induced conformational changes in CP at the actin-binding interface are less extensive than those induced by CARMIL, consistent with CARMIL (but not mTwf1) weakening CP binding to actin barbed ends.
results.evaluation: This inference from HDX-MS data (C96, Figure 5) is consistent with the functional differences between Twinfilin and CARMIL: CARMIL displaces CP from barbed ends while Twinfilin does not. The HDX-MS data show differential protection patterns at the actin-binding interface. This structural observation provides a mechanistic explanation for the functional differences observed in other experiments.

results.result: A revised model for the CP regulatory cycle is proposed in which: (1) Twinfilin protects CP from V-1, maintaining a larger pool of active Twinfilin-CP complexes in the cytosol; (2) V-1 maintains a reservoir of inactive CP that can be mobilized by Twinfilin or CARMIL; (3) Twinfilin-CP complexes provide stable capping while CARMIL-CP complexes provide transient capping at the membrane; (4) Twinfilin-CP association primes filaments for disassembly, with CARMIL potentially displacing CP to leave Twinfilin at barbed ends for depolymerization.
results.evaluation: This is a speculative model (C123-C129, Figure 7D) that integrates the experimental findings but extends beyond what is directly demonstrated. While the model is consistent with the data and provides testable hypotheses, key aspects remain unproven: the relative pools of different CP complexes in cells, the spatial organization of these pools, and the proposed mechanism of priming for disassembly. The model represents reasonable speculation but requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: A structural model suggests that the Twinfilin tail is long enough to allow simultaneous binding of its CPI motif to CP and its C-terminal ADFH domain to an actin subunit at the barbed end, with no steric clashes. CP and Twinfilin can associate with barbed ends individually or as a complex, with distinct functional consequences. CP-Twinfilin complexes may stably cap barbed ends similar to CP alone.
results.evaluation: The structural model (C134-C135, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) is based on docking known structures and is plausible but not experimentally validated. The proposal that CP-Twinfilin complexes can simultaneously bind barbed ends (C136, C138) is speculative and not directly tested. While the model is consistent with the linker length and known structures, it requires experimental validation such as cryo-EM or direct functional assays of the ternary complex.

results.result: Background on Twinfilin: It is one of five proteins in the ADF-H domain family, unique in containing two ADF-H domains. Initially characterized as an actin monomer sequestering factor, it was later shown to interact with barbed ends and accelerate depolymerization. Both yeast and mammalian Twinfilins bind CP with high affinity (~10 nM for yeast), mediated by conserved C-terminal tail sequences, though previous studies found no significant effects of Twinfilin on CP capping activity or vice versa.
results.evaluation: These are literature review claims (C9-C27) supported by appropriate citations to prior work. They establish the context and prior knowledge state before the current study. The apparent paradox of high-affinity binding without functional consequences (C25-C27) motivates the current investigation. These claims are properly attributed to prior work and provide necessary background.

results.result: Background on CP and its regulation: CP is an obligate heterodimer that stably caps barbed ends with sub-nanomolar affinity and slow dissociation (t1/2 ~30 min). It is ubiquitous, highly conserved, and present at 1-3 µM in cells. CP inhibitors fall into two classes: steric inhibitors (V-1) that block CP binding to barbed ends, and allosteric inhibitors (CPI-motif proteins like CARMIL) that catalyze CP dissociation and reduce its affinity ~100-fold. Prior to this study, no 'pro-capping' factors that antagonize CP inhibitors had been reported.
results.evaluation: These are literature review claims (C28-C49) establishing the state of knowledge about CP regulation prior to this study. They are supported by appropriate citations and provide essential context. The statement that no pro-capping factors were known (C49) sets up the novelty of the current findings. These background claims are accurate representations of prior work.

results.result: Background on V-1 mechanism: V-1 does not displace CP from barbed ends but sequesters CP and blocks it from binding filament ends. V-1 binds CP on the opposite face from CARMIL, sterically blocking barbed end binding. CARMIL can form a transient ternary complex with V-1 and CP, accelerating V-1 dissociation.
results.evaluation: These are literature review claims (C81-C82, C88) supported by appropriate citations to prior structural and functional studies. They provide important mechanistic context for understanding how Twinfilin's effects on V-1 (demonstrated in this study) relate to CARMIL's known effects. The citations are appropriate and the claims accurately represent prior work.

results.result: Summary and evolutionary conservation: The functions of mammalian Twinfilin and CP are closely intertwined, and this relationship likely extends to other species given sequence conservation and the conserved nature of the Twinfilin-CP interaction. S. cerevisiae Aim21 was recently identified as the first yeast CPI motif-containing protein that regulates CP at cortical actin patches.
results.evaluation: The summary statement (C130) is justified by the collective experimental data. The evolutionary conservation argument (C131) is reasonable given the sequence alignment data (Figure 2A) and known conservation of the interaction. The reference to yeast Aim21 (C132-C133) provides relevant context showing that CPI-mediated CP regulation exists in yeast, supporting the evolutionary conservation argument.

results.result: Broader implications: When Twinfilin alone associates with barbed ends, it drives processive depolymerization while blocking assembly. Despite differences in their barbed end associations, CP and Twinfilin each inhibit filament growth, explaining why Twinfilin can replace CP in reconstituted motility assays. Actin dynamics are controlled by complex multi-component mechanisms at barbed ends, allowing rapid transitions through different functional states. These mechanisms are more elaborate than previously thought.
results.evaluation: These discussion points (C139-C144) integrate the current findings with broader knowledge of actin regulation. The statement about Twinfilin driving depolymerization (C139) is supported by prior citations. The functional similarity between CP and Twinfilin in blocking growth (C140-C141) is a reasonable inference that explains prior observations. The broader perspective on actin regulation (C142-C144) is appropriate synthesis and speculation based on the findings.
